Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) exhibits life-history traits characteristic of a capital-breeding viperid adapted to seasonal tropical environments. Field studies have documented that neonates emerge from leathery-shelled eggs at a total length of approximately 27 centimeters [Lb = approximately 27 centimeters], a size that reflects substantial yolk provisioning during embryonic development. This initial body size is critical for juvenile survival, as it determines the range of prey items a young-of-year reptile can subdue. Following the onset of exogenous feeding, hatchlings enter a period of rapid somatic growth that continues through the juvenile stage. The species attains an ultimate total length of approximately 166 centimeters [Li = approximately 166 centimeters], a measurement that represents the maximum recorded body size among adults in wild populations across the Indian subcontinent. This large adult size, uncommon among regional viperids, is associated with a diet that shifts from arthropods and small lizards in juveniles to small mammals and birds in adults. The growth trajectory from the hatchling length of about 27 centimeters to the adult maximum of 166 centimeters spans several years and is influenced by seasonal prey abundance and thermoregulatory opportunities available in the species' diverse habitats.

Reproductive development in Russell's viper proceeds relatively slowly compared to many other snake species of similar body size. Under controlled thermal conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], individuals reach the size associated with the attainment of sexual maturity at a total length of 100 centimeters [Lp = 100 centimeters]. This length at puberty, approximately 60 percent of the ultimate adult length, represents a substantial somatic investment before individuals become capable of reproduction. The age at which this size threshold is reached, estimated at 690 days [tR = 690 days] under the same thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], indicates that the first reproduction event occurs well into the second year of life. This relatively delayed onset of breeding, compared to smaller viperid species, is likely linked to the energetic demands of achieving a body length sufficient to accommodate large mammalian prey items and to store adequate fat reserves for vitellogenesis. Data from captive colonies consistently demonstrate that individuals maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] do not exhibit evidence of gonadal activation before reaching this age and length combination.

The reproductive output of Daboia russelii reflects its high capital investment strategy, where females convert stored energy reserves into large, yolked litters. At a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] in captivity, females typically produce a single clutch annually, yielding an average of 30 offspring per year [Ri = 30 offspring per year]. This pattern of infrequent but large litters is typical of viperid snakes and reflects the physiological costs of yolk synthesis and gestation. The production of approximately 30 live-born offspring per event places Russell's viper among the more fecund viperine species, a feature that may compensate for relatively high juvenile mortality rates in the wild. The thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] under which these data were collected represents a common laboratory standard that approximates mean annual soil temperatures in the species' range.

Incubation conditions profoundly affect early life-history parameters in Daboia russelii, particularly the duration of embryonic development. At the standard laboratory temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the gestation period from ovum activation through yolk-dependent embryogenesis to the emergence of live neonates spans approximately 183 days [ab = approximately 183 days], a value derived from six months of constant thermal exposure. This developmental duration is consistent with the prolonged incubation periods observed in other large-bodied viperid snakes and is directly linked to the metabolic rate of the leathery-shelled egg. The embryonic development within the eggshell proceeds slowly at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], allowing for thorough yolk utilization before the transition to exogenous feeding. Newborn snakes emerge with a total length near 27 centimeters [Lb = 27 centimeters], as mentioned earlier, and immediately begin active foraging. The substantial length at birth provides a survival advantage, enabling neonates to capture relatively large prey compared to the smaller hatchlings of many colubrid species that share the same geographic range.

Longevity in Russell's viper under captive conditions, when maintained at a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], has been documented to reach approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This maximum lifespan is moderately long for a snake of this body size, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances extended reproductive opportunities against the accumulated risks of senescence in a predator-rich environment. The 15-year lifespan, combined with the onset of first reproduction at around 690 days [tR = around 690 days] and an annual reproductive output of 30 offspring per year [Ri = 30 offspring per year], yields a lifetime reproductive output that can exceed 400 offspring under optimal con at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]ditions. This demographic pattern, characterized by delayed maturity and high per-event fecundity, is consistent with a bet-hedging strategy adapted to variable juvenile survival. Field records from long-term mark-recapture studies in southern India corroborate these captive longevity estimates, suggesting that the species' physiological constraints at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] are broadly representative of natural thermal conditions in the wild.
